speaker: The Chairman
text: If you could just take your first cut.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will prepare us to bolster our hub status as a reliable and resilient transport node to the world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, there is a general consensus that digitalisation is required to mitigate the risk of supply chain disruptions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To utilise our limited resources productively, we have already been focusing on digitalisation before the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, the unpredictability of supply chain disruptions has led businesses to move from "just in time" to a "just in case" inventory strategy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As businesses start to keep a fair level of buffer beyond their expected inventory needs, they are also looking for integrated short-term storage solutions in addition to the efficient processing and clearance of goods at our ports.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This creates a conundrum for land-scarce Singapore, where storage space at our ports or elsewhere is only available at a premium.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, we must remember that supply chain disruptions are a global problem and no one country is going to solve it themselves.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Even as we compete, we must recognise that sharing knowledge and solutions will improve the interoperability across a network of ports and enhance our resilience and reliability as a regional transport solution.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Through this pandemic, I am glad that we have succeeded in developing and sharing safe crew change protocols with fellow International Maritime Organisation member states and enhanced our digital OCEANSTM initiative to shape and harmonise global data standards.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must continue these efforts to export knowledge.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Mr Chairman, today, many countries in the world are talking about smart transportation or intelligent transportation systems.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Time-wise, we are almost at the 50% mark.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Could the Ministry share an update on our progress?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: What are the Ministry's plan and strategy to embrace, testbed and utilise new and advanced technologies to benefit commuters in Singapore or even globally?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Putting aside autonomous and green vehicles, one of the centrepieces in the Smart Mobility vision is to leverage data and analytics to optimise the use of transport systems.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Besides collecting information and analysing them at the backend, it is equally important to push such information to individual commuters, so that we are able to influence our user behaviour in real time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This is not new – we have long been informing motorists of road conditions through radio broadcasts and the Expressway Monitoring and Advisory System’s (EMAS) electronic signboards.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: However, rapid improvements in technology mean there are now faster and more efficient ways to push information to commuters.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We can now look to apps and websites on our mobile phone for bus arrival timings from the SBS Transit app, ERP rates from the MyTransport app and road conditions from OneMotoring.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But these are only as useful as we can get commuters to use them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: What is the utilisation of feedback on these informative apps?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: For example, at the usage of Park Connector Network (PCN) level, we can roll out a PCN cycling and pedestrian density real-time "crowd level" map akin to NParks' Safe Distance website where it helps users avoid or navigate with the understanding it is a busy PCN peak period.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We are seeing these exciting transport evolutions as we see the transport industry facing a sea change globally.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Technological advancements are driving the evolution of smart and intelligent transport systems.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We are seeing these exciting transport evolutions in Singapore as well, including the Hyundai electric vehicle (EV) plant that is coming up, the commercial air taxi services that are coming up as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Smart technology can complement our transport system by providing last-mile connectivity where required, such as to our islands.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: At the same time, the COVID-19 pandemic has also shaken up the transport industry over the past two years as transport routes and norms are disrupted.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: What is the projected job creation outlook in the transport sector, be it air, land or maritime?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: What are the emerging areas and what future jobs will be there and how can we encourage and develop local talent to join these sectors early on?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Melvin Yong, take both your cuts together.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Chairman, the COVID-19 pandemic has a profound impact on our transport workforce across the air, sea and land sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: First, it is no secret that our aviation sector has been hard hit by the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But as more vaccinated travel lane arrangements are made and air travel starts to recover, what is the Government's outlook for the aviation sector?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Is the worst behind us or are we looking at a long bottom of a U-shape recovery curve?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It takes years to train our aviation staff, especially highly-skilled jobs, such as pilots and aircraft technicians.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A well-trained and well-staffed workforce is vital for Singapore to recover our status as a travel hub.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How does the Government intend to support the aviation sector and revive Changi Airport's manpower capacity?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Are there any plans to increase recruitment to prepare for the return of air travel demand?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Our maritime sector, however, has done well amidst the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Singapore's ports handled a record number of container throughput in 2021.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As the sector grows and transforms, what are the Ministry's plans to attract more local workers to join the maritime sector?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Has the enhanced Career Conversion Programme for Sea Transport Professionals and Associates been successful in attracting Singaporeans into this growth sector?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Lastly, our land transport sector saw more locals joining as bus captains, bus technicians and rail engineers in the past two years, many of whom are mid-career switchers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But as our economy recovers and companies in the hospitality and tourism industries ask ex-staff to return, do we foresee an increase in attrition among our public transport workforce?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How does the Ministry intend to tackle this attrition and keep our essential services attractive to Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We should build a reserve public bus captain pool, one that can be activated upon short notice to fill urgent manpower gaps.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I propose to train taxi drivers to act as reserve bus captains.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This reserve force could drive buses once a month to keep their driving skills and route familiarity current so that they can be activated upon an emergency.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Two of our public bus operators, SBS Transit and SMRT, have taxi companies within their corporate groups today.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope LTA can work with the National Transport Workers' Union (NTWU) to initiate a pilot with these two companies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: COVID-19 has fundamentally changed the way we live, work and play.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: My concern is whether we need to review our pre-pandemic key planning parameters for our major transport infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How will the permanent shifts in the way we live and work affect our long-term plans to grow the MRT network?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on our rail expansion plans, specifically, the Cross Island and Jurong Regional Lines, and whether we need to review the earlier ridership projections for these lines?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Our aviation sector, too, has seen a continued slump and the Ministry had announced a two-year pause in Changi Airport Terminal 5's construction.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on when construction will resume, if at all, and whether there will be changes to the scope of the project?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Lastly, the maritime sector, however, has performed well amidst the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Chairman, the pandemic has completely changed our lives in the past two years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: There may not be an exact endpoint where we can say life is going back to normal.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: While we are slowly restoring parts of our lives, some parts have changed forever.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Before I proceed, I would like to declare my interest as I am working in the land transport industry.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is amazing how all of us have been forced to work from home in one way or another in the past two years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Will working from home be a permanent feature in the future?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: More employers are also willing to have their workers put on staggered working hours.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Indeed, data from a study in San Francisco showed that the pandemic had reduced traffic throughout the morning peak hour and spread it all over throughout the day.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Ultimately, this can also contribute to healthier communities as there is less air pollution and is aligned with our green plan.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Therefore, we need to capitalise on the work-from-home trend to permanently reduce the level of travel demand during the peak hours between 7.30 am and 9.30 am.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Before the pandemic, the resources devoted to the morning peak hours often defined the maximum capacity required to meet the travel demand.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If there is a need to have an early meeting at 8.00 am, perhaps we can allow some of them to join the meeting virtually.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The unions can also chip in to encourage similar practices in the private sector.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In London, some national rail services do not stop at the busiest interchanges at peak times in a deliberate attempt to discourage travelling during peak hours.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But I do not suggest that Singapore do the same.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It might be better for PTC to amend the fare structure to give a significant discount during the off-peak travel period.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, providing monetary incentives alone will not shift the travel pattern significantly.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: There was only a sustained decrease of about 7% of commuters exiting the 16 participating MRT stations during the peak period between 8.00 am and 9.00 am.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This means that there needs to be a combination of people working from home, staggered working hours and financial incentives for off-peak travelling to result in a significant and sustained impact.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: After going through the pandemic, I hope MOT can work with the various stakeholders to cement the change.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This will also mean a more pleasant ride on our trains and buses.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If we manage to flatten the curve of peak-hour travelling, should we allow or should we slow down the construction of MRT lines?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I hope MOT will reply with a firm "no".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: After the construction of the North-East Line, when the ridership was much lower than what LTA had anticipated, the construction of the Circle Line and Downtown Line was delayed.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: That resulted in overcrowding in the oldest North-South and East-West lines.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We should not create the same kind of situation again.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We should still build train lines ahead of demand.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I trust that MOT will continue with its plan for the Jurong Regional Line and Cross Island Line.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, we can consider reducing the number of trains deployed to save on the operating, maintenance and fixed asset costs, like rolling stock, if we are successful in flattening the peak-hour travel demand.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Next, I would like to move on to the topic of cycling.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The pandemic has made cycling more popular for leisure and for commuting.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, these paths and the park connector network, or PCN, are getting crowded as more Singaporeans are using them.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I have come across instances where the entire shared path was blocked by families holding hands and walking in a row side-by-side.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: On other occasions, I had also seen three bicycles cycling in parallel, blocking the entire PCN.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: To keep everyone safe, I suggest that there should be dedicated cycling and pedestrian paths as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: East Coast Park is one of those parks which have dedicated cycling and pedestrian paths and we need to extend this to more places, such as the PCNs in Marina Bay, Alexandra or the Sengkang/Punggol PCN and more.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In order to create separate paths, the entire path needs to be widened to include the space on either side.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Hence, the agencies need to be bold to take back the land or to repurpose the land which may now comprise part of a road or a grass verge to expand the PCN.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: COVID-19 might have slowed down our pursuit of new technologies in transport, such as autonomous vehicle or AVs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The use of AVs is an important technological milestone that we cannot miss.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In 2020, Singapore was named as the world's top country for autonomous driving due to the expansion of our testing areas and training of bus drivers to operate AVs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In fact, there was an earlier announcement that three new towns would be served by driverless buses by 2022.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The aviation sector has been badly impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the travel sector gradually recovers, how fast can Changi Airport open up to more Vaccinated Travel Lanes (VTLs)?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the Government support our airport to recover its role as an aviation hub safely?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the longer term, how will the airport continue to remain competitive and provide good jobs for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As almost all Singaporeans and residents complete their vaccinations and boosters or acquire immunity, it will become safer for our travel sector to resume.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Minister provide an update on the upcoming plans to reopen our borders and attract more flights to Changi Airport?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry share its outlook for the aviation sector for 2022?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: On the home side, Singaporeans have become a little stir-crazy from restricted travel overseas for leisure, and business persons are also looking for easier travel procedures to places they need to be at.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I would like to ask the Minister about MOT's plans to recover air passenger travel and revive the aviation sector.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: On a related note, I would also like to ask if there are plans to ultimately drop the VTL system and to introduce quarantine-free travel for vaccinated travellers from all destinations, perhaps starting with vaccinated Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, may I take my two cuts together?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to first declare my interest as an Executive in the Changi Airport Group.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: The aviation sector has been one of the hardest hit by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Although the spread of the Omicron variant has been a drag on the recovery of the sector, there was still cautious optimism at the beginning of this year that global air travel demand will pick up over the course of 2022.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Unfortunately, the war in Ukraine has now cast a shadow over the much-anticipated recovery of this sector.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Flights over Europe may also need to be rerouted due to the war.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Would the Ministry share its views on these events and their impact and its outlook for the aviation sector?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What is our strategy going forward to minimise the impact of the pandemic and the war on our aviation sector?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Despite these challenges, we should try to proceed to open our borders safely.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Will the Ministry provide an update on the upcoming plans to reopen our borders?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: With different countries issuing different travel regulations in their attempts to control the pandemic, air travel has become challenging and fraught with confusion.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: A uniform set of travel regulations would be more helpful to rejuvenate air travel.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What is the Ministry's view on this and what can Singapore do to contribute to improve cooperation with our partner countries, especially those with the most traffic with Singapore?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: After more than two years of the pandemic, how many workers were still employed at the end of 2021?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: With the gradual resumption of travel, how can the Government ensure that there are sufficient workers to cope with the border reopening?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What are the measures to increase the automation of labour-intensive jobs?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: In the longer term, how can we ensure that the aviation sector remains attractive and provides good jobs?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How will the Government continue to support the sector to scale up its capacity and capabilities?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Would the Ministry share more about its plans under the blueprint?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Companies in the aviation sector are trying to keep afloat amidst a very difficult environment caused by the prolonged COVID-19 pandemic and, now, the war in Ukraine, which will lead to higher oil prices.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What will the Government do to help the aviation sector cope with increased carbon taxes in addition to the other cost pressures?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What grants and funds are available for the aviation industry to invest in new technology and equipment that will reduce carbon emissions and boost energy efficiency?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Dennis Tan, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the last few months, there appears to be some lamentation over the slow recovery of the Asia Pacific aviation industry from the pandemic amidst government restrictions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: According to IATA, the region is the only part of the world to see practically no improvement in air travel during the past year.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A few months on, as countries battled their way out of the Omicron threat, I wonder whether there is any sign of recovery for the aviation industry in the Asia Pacific and, indeed, for Singapore this year.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At last year's Committee of Supply (COS), Minister Ong Ye Kung told the House not to expect a V-shaped recovery.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: That was before the start of the VTLs for Singapore and many other countries.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many countries have relaxed travel restrictions in the last few months.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Nearer home, Singapore continues to increase its VTL locations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Australia recently opened its borders to visitors again.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As more countries start to open up and increase flights to other countries and with some relaxing COVID-19 test requirements, will the Minister update the House on his expectations for growth of air travel in the coming year and its implications for Singapore as a major air hub and for our aviation industry?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would also like to ask the Minister whether we will see the start of recovery for the aerospace sector.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This sector is significant to Singapore and includes maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO), avionics and aircraft component production and repair.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As we head towards a post-pandemic world, may I also take the opportunity to ask the Minister whether he can update the House on MOT's review of its plans for Terminal 5?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Mr Chairman, I declare my interest as a maritime lawyer.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In August 2021, the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) was set up by the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) and six partner maritime organisations and companies to, I quote, "Support decarbonisation of the maritime industry to meet or exceed the International Maritime Organisation (IMO)'s goals for 2030 and 2050." Its stated goals were, among other things, and I quote again, "Lower the adoption barriers for low zero carbon fuels and technologies by closing the gaps in infrastructure, safety operations and financing, and to accelerate the deployment of scalable low-carbon technologies." The opening of the Centre and the Centre's aims are, indeed, befitting of our port as a leading bunkering port in the world as well as one of the busiest ports in the world and one of the major world maritime hubs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Singapore should aim to take the lead to hasten the development and adoption of low- or zero-carbon fuels for commercial shipping at this critical time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The International Advisory Panel on Maritime Decarbonisation had earlier proposed the establishment of this Global Maritime/Decarbonisation Centre in Singapore to coordinate, drive and catalyse maritime decarbonisation solutions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It was reported that Singapore commenced regular ship-to-ship LNG bunkering operations from March last year and that Singapore will continue to diversify our fuel offerings in line with our push for maritime decarbonisation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Indeed, LNG itself may not even be a long-term solution.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The industry may have to push on to better low, if not zero, carbon fuels.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There is not much time for all stakeholders in the maritime industry in the world to achieve the goals set by IMO to halve greenhouse emissions from 2008 levels by 2050.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There is much to do in our search for affordable zero-carbon fuels.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope GCMD will enable Singapore to spearhead the push among leading maritime nations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will the Minister share with this House his hopes for GCMD and also his expectation of what Singapore hopes to achieve for its bunker sales in terms of lower carbon offerings in the coming five, 10 and perhaps 20 years?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Public transport remains the main mode of commute for the majority of Singaporeans and LTA needs to ensure that our public transport remains, safe, reliable, accessible and comfortable.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And, yet, at the same time, I urge the Ministry to ensure that public transport remains affordable, as it is a public service available to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, may I ask the Minister whether there is any assessment or evaluation as to the reasons for the drop in commuter satisfaction?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What are the steps taken by public transport operators to improve on their performance?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Would a report be issued by the public transport operators on their remedial action?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Here, I declare my interest in this Thomson-East Line as there will be four MRT stations located in my constituency.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Chairman, what has been the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on our plan to grow the MRT network from 230 kilometres to 360 kilometres in the early 2030s?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Would the Ministry share what is the progress of the feasibility study of the new lines, including the possibility to have a line to serve the residents in Buangkok, Yio Chu Kang, Fernvale and Punggol?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This has resulted in my residents having to put up with longer waiting times, crowded buses and losing direct routes to their destinations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If bus services are being rationalised due to low ridership, I would like to suggest that LTA first consider switching to smaller buses or extending their headways.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If bus services must be removed, the frequency of the remaining feeder services to bus interchanges or MRT stations should be increased to make up for them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: LTA should strive to retain trunk bus services.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These serve many elderly and disabled residents who have trouble walking between bus stops or transferring from bus to MRT.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many of them do not mind longer bus routes or bus rides if that allows them to walk less.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While LTA and public transport operators strive towards efficiency, they must pay closer attention to the comfort and convenience of commuters.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: LTA should proactively monitor public feedback and be open to bringing back bus services if there is strong commuter demand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On its face, this sounds like a preposterous and profligate idea.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Preposterous, because, surely, removing charges would invite overuse and abuse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Profligate, because even when they are made free of charge, these services are, certainly, not free of cost and must be funded by some source – in this case, the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But before we jump to instinctive judgement, it is worth noting that free ridership already exists in some form or another.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In Singapore, there are free transport shuttles for patrons of Turf City, for tourists seeking a city tour during a stopover and for students connecting to campus from nearby MRT stations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some municipalities from smaller ones, such as Hoeselt in Belgium and Obare in France, to larger cities, such as Prague in the Czech Republic and Washington DC in the United States, run selected free bus and tram services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Tallinn, the capital city of Estonia, recently converted its entire public transportation network to a zero-fare system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Around two years ago, Luxembourg became the first nation in the world to make all public transportation modes free within the country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As our society ages, but many elderly remain mobile and healthy, some may wish to continue to pursue employment opportunities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such positions, typically on a part-time basis, do not pay very much and public transportation would very quickly gobble up a sufficiently large share of the pay cheque, so as to make the entire enterprise no longer worthwhile.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Free transport for seniors will allow those who wish to remain productive and engage in employment to do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our labour force participation has already trended down since 2015 and while this is natural and normal in an ageing society, the scheme will help mitigate the rate of decline and allow our economy time to adjust.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even in the absence of work, free transport will encourage the elderly to be out and about, engaging in social interactions that can promote their physical and mental well-being.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This can help manage the rising incidence of dementia, which already one in every 10 seniors faces.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This initiative also dovetails nicely with our nation's effort to promote environmental sustainability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: An important cornerstone of the Singapore Green Plan 2030 is to encourage green commutes, with a target of 75% mass public transportation usage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Providing incentives for our elderly and disabled to rely more heavily on public transport, since trips will be free, will contribute toward this goal, especially since riders are least likely to be using green forms of transportation, such as bicycles, in any case.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: An initiative, such as this, will entail trade-offs, of course.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our existing pricing structure is, to be fair, relatively affordable by global standards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, seniors and the disabled already pay concessionary rates on existing tariffs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government has also invested heavily in the transportation infrastructure on which the public transportation system relies on, thereby providing an indirect subsidy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But to the extent that fares are used to offset operational costs, with profits subject to corporate taxation and dividends returned to majority shareholders, such as Temasek, the Government is able to recoup much of its initial outlay.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Seniors and the disabled are only a comparatively small fraction of public transportation ridership.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The financial impact would, therefore, correspondingly be much more limited.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If so, the opportunity cost of not implementing such a free transportation scheme may well exceed the cost of doing so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Mr Chairman, LTA has declared that it seeks, and I quote: "inclusive public transportation system", one that ensures barrier-free access for wheelchairs and strollers, providing priority boarding lines and reserved seats for elderly and disabled commuters and creating bus-stop seats that are more elderly-friendly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While these multidimensional aspects of inclusivity exist, we have neglected inclusion of the most fundamental form – ensuring free access to public transport for those who can least afford it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some have gone as far as to argue that urban transit is a human right, akin to why we do not pay to ride elevators.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY – HEAD W (MINISTRY OF TRANSPORT) (Creating an inclusive and sustainable home)

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Mr Chairman, I have raised on multiple occasions in this House about the importance of ensuring that our workers travel to and from work safely every day.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: The Government had said that it was reviewing how to enhance the safety of workers ferried in the rear decks of lorries after a spate of traffic accidents last year.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on this as well as to my earlier suggestions to install speed limiters and seat belts, as interim measures, on lorries used to ferry workers to enhance safety?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These prices impact persons from low-income background, especially those who use motorcycles as part of their work.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For them, taking public transport is not a viable option.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Even as demand for these continue to be strong, the supply has been squeezed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In these current circumstances, motorcycle prices may rise even further unless something is done.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I support a cap on our vehicles, as the number on our roads draw near to one million, but I wonder if the total number can be allocated differently.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wonder if the Government is prepared to recognise a separate category of delivery motorcycles and apply a similar growth rate for this category.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This may go some way to mitigate the high COE prices for motorcycles used for work.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is a practical and fair way to harness the market to work for us.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, the cost of owning a motorcycle has risen miserably for motorcycle riders since the past year, more so with COEs for motorcycles crossing the $10,000 mark.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This has impacted many workers riding small motorcycles, not just to and from work but also for those who use it to earn a living, to bring food on the table for themselves and their family members.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Many of my cousins, friends, union members and fellow workers shared with me their concerns and they are worried about how the cost of owning a motorcycle would affect their livelihood.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Not more than three years ago, the cost of purchasing a new motorcycle with a small engine capacity is around $8,000 or below, including with COE.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: But today, it is a really big challenge for them.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: MOT certainly has the data of motorcycle ownerships based on engine capacity.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, on behalf of all of them, I am appealing that MOT takes a much deeper and closer look and provide the necessary support or assistance for this group of riders.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Can MOT also consider tiering the COE prices based on engine capacity?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: To the Minister for Transport, this is the plea I wish to convey on behalf of them: "We like to earn a living for ourselves and family and this is only what we can afford.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: If you don't help us, who then should we turn to, Sir?"

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And how does it impact those who are dependent on motorcycles for their livelihoods?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Motorcycles is one the essential mode of transport that have helped many meet many critical and general business needs, such as delivery and dispatch of goods and documents.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is less impacted by traffic jams and hence, can be a more reliable transport mode to get around, including delivering essential items like medicines or attending to emergency repairs and many other economic activities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many full-time and freelance workers are also dependent on their motorcycles for livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, the sharp rise in COE premiums do cause anxieties to these riders.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Their concerns are whether would the COE premium continue to rise higher and to stay high.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Like any markets, there is always room for interventions when the price actions do not reflect fundamentals, or where there are market distortions that cause imbalances in demand and supply.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What are the reasons for the recent record high premiums of motorcycle COEs?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What can the Government do to moderate or bring down the premiums to more affordable levels?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Should we look at the supply of the motorcycles' COE as one way to meet the higher demand?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Otherwise, would the Government consider other additional measures to help those who are impacted and dependent on their motorcycles for livelihoods?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Chairman, in previous Budgets, COS debates and Parliamentary Questions (PQs), I have spoken about whether the Government can do more regarding the high prices of motorcycle COEs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: High demand, like what my Parliamentary colleagues have just mentioned, is one of the reasons.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Another possible reason is that over the years, there was a reduction of the percentage of total COEs used by motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And this is because a portion of motorcycle COEs were converted previously into Open Category COEs, even though motorists rarely used the Open Category COEs for motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I previously asked for MOT to consider stopping this transfer to Open Category and for a greater proportion of COEs to be allocated to motorcycles over time, with an eye of restoring the original ratio of motorcycle versus non-motorcycle COEs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, over the years, the Government has conducted several reviews of regulations to ensure safe usage of active mobility devices.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Active mobility modes have also increased in popularity since the pandemic started.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Would the Ministry provide an update on the situation today?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: How many Singaporeans and residents are using active mobility devices on a regular basis today, compared to the last two years?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What are the Government’s plans to support active mobility while ensuring safety for all users and pedestrians?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Would the Ministry provide an update on the Islandwide Cycling Network?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With the rise in the number of cyclists for commuting, delivery and leisure, would the Government speed up the construction of cycling networks, especially in towns with dense cycling traffic?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Mr Chairman, in the past half a year or possibly longer, I have noted from media websites that the authorities have been regularly conducting operations to promote safe riding efforts by cyclists and Personal Mobility Devices (PMD) users.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And according to news, media reports or the LTA Facebook page, these efforts included enforcement against errant riders, as well as efforts by officers to stop and engage riders on-the-ground on safe riding etiquette, as well as use of the right equipment, such as having compliant e-bikes complying with road traffic or active mobility rules – such as observing appropriate speed limits, complying with traffic lights, riding against the traffic, no riding on expressways, wearing of helmets and riding in the right numbers or formation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I had previously spoken of the need for consistent enforcement and I am heartened by the publicity on more regular enforcement.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The enhanced publicity for these operations and engagements are also good, as they should help to encourage riders to be more conscious in riding safely and complying with road traffic or active mobility rules.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While I agree that the recent efforts are a step in the right direction, I have continued to see, on quite a regular basis, that there are still riders who, for example, beat red lights or cycle against the traffic, or do not wear helmets and riding on the road.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I still see some e-scooters on the road or on footpaths, even though their use on these services have been banned for some time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Though I agree that the use of PMDs on roads or footpaths have reduced considerably from the time before the ban took place, I am often surprised to see that people continue to take the risk of riding illegally.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In particular, are there any lessons learned from the enforcement or engagement efforts in recent months, which can be applied to persuade this group of active mobility users?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: With Singapore moving towards being a car-lite society, as well as the COVID-19 pandemic leading to a cycling boom, there have been many altercations between motorists and cyclists in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: These incidences may be uploaded on social media, which serves to stoke further tensions between them.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It can help protect the cyclists when accidents occur, providing compensation for victims of accidents.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: As such, I would like to find out the timeframe for rolling out these measures.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Even though the Panel has decided not to license on-road cyclists, public education is still an important part of the adoption of these recommendations.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: There is also a concurrent need to educate the drivers as well.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Motorists may not be aware of what cyclists can do on the road and not all cyclists are familiar with the highway code.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: What will the Ministry be doing to step up public education on road safety for cyclists and motorists hand-in-hand with its enforcement action?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, there is already an extensive network of island-wide bicycle-friendly trails, comprising the Park Connector Network (PCN), alongside trails as well as corridors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But these trails do no address the so-called "Last Mile Problem", where riders are still required to ride on regular roads and occasionally on pavements, to the detriment of some of the Members of this House as well as safety, to get to their final destination, or to traverse across the estate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Bicycle riders can, of course, make use of existing roads, riding to the far left.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But when bike lanes are not designated, there is an absence of clear guidelines for vehicle drivers and this often results in compromising the riders' safety when passing vehicles leave uncomfortably little space.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Accordingly, riders ride defensively, sometimes two abreast, to occupy the entire lane, which would be more inefficient than designating a clear, even if narrow, bike lane and correspondingly narrow lines for regular vehicles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Since cycling paths currently allow the use of powered vehicles, delivery riders that cannot ply foot paths, will have a safe alternative for their Personal Mobility Devices (PMDs).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In Sengkang, such delivery riders and dedicated bike lanes seem like a win-win solution that will accommodate our many PMD users.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such bike lanes will also encourage activities that promote environmental sustainability.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Their inconsiderate behaviour is a cause of danger to other users of the shared paths or foot paths, who may be injured by such riders.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I have seen regular enforcement action taken by LTA and NParks' officers, but this situation does not seem to have improved.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The enforcement officers cannot possibly be at the park connector or other shared paths every day.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Pedestrians tell me they do not feel safe using the shared paths or footpaths, when cyclists zip by them at high speeds and in a dangerous manner.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And this is especially so for pedestrians who are seniors or with young toddlers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: One wrong step by the toddler or the senior person may mean serious injury if a speeding bicycle crashes on them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It does not help that many shared paths do not have clear demarcation as to which side of the path is for pedestrians and which side is for the cyclists.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Indeed, I myself have walked along such paths and I felt it was very stressful not knowing whether a reckless cyclist would crash into my back.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In Tanjong Rhu, there used to be a sign – a small sign – that the cyclists are not supposed to ride beyond the bicycle lane.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But when a prominent "No Cycling" sign was put on the floor of the footpath bridge, I saw marked improvements in the behaviours of cyclists and a large majority of cyclists dismounted and pushed their bicycles across the foot path.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Without the prominent signage, many cyclists would just ride across the bridge.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: They do not feel that their safety is threatened.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: This is the combined efforts of MHA, which maintains a very low crime level in Singapore and the concerted planning and execution of various Ministries, like MND and MOT.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I am a member of the Discover Tanjong Pagar Business Improvement District (BID), which is an association of private development stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We work together to find ways to enhance the Tanjong Pagar neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Initially seeded by MND and URA, the Discover Tanjong Pagar BID has become a close-knit group of stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The BID had many positive experiences working with the agencies, such as URA, NParks, SLA, PA and LTA.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: On walkability, members of the BID had site walks with LTA officers to explain some of the areas of concerns for pedestrian safety or comfort.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: With the other agencies, we have jointly developed green spaces, introduced play facilities and tree planting.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: LTA considered the inputs from the BID and implemented improvements, such as introducing new traffic lights or widening of footpaths.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: These efforts cannot make news headlines, but they relate to the detailed on-the-ground adjustments that greatly improve the experience of the neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Can MOT share more about how agencies and stakeholders can work together to make our city more walkable, vibrant and liveable?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More Singaporeans and residents are taking up cycling as a form of exercise and as a green mode of transport.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our road network spans 9,000 lane-kilometres and requires much maintenance to keep it in good and safe condition.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the face of labour shortage, how would LTA upkeep maintenance?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will LTA be leveraging on new technology or materials to maintain this network effectively?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Illegally-modified vehicles cause not only noise pollution, which disturb residents, especially late at night.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They also put the drivers, passengers and other road users at risk.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There have been quite a number of incidents where they either burst into flames or would not be able to function safely.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is LTA doing to address this problem of illegally-modified vehicles and motorcycles?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Through the years, our taxi and private hire vehicle driving community has been keeping Singapore going.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Rain or shine, early mornings and late nights, pandemic or no pandemic, providing a reliable and safe form of transportation for many Singaporean families.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our resilient hardworking drivers have weathered changes to their industry, affecting their livelihoods and lives.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some changes are sudden, like COVID-19; some changes are long-tailed, like technology changes, ranging from changing diesel standards, the invention of ride-hailing apps, the rolling out of full EV vehicles.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our drivers have rolled with the times and, with the support and representation of the NTUC Associations, National Taxi Association and the National Private Hire Vehicles Association, their resilience and courage have carried them out of these situations stronger and better.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the midst of the fuel price surges, which have left our drivers reeling and frightened about the sustainability of their livelihoods, our association leaders have led the charge and bringing the matter of business cost up to the taxi and ride-hail platform partners as well as LTA.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our leaders have similarly worked with the tripartite partners in the introduction and extension of the COVID-19 Driver Relief Fund (CDRF), which has given our drivers some added measure of relief.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One evergreen challenge our leaders have brought up is the support needed to aid drivers looking to transit out of driving.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unlike salaried employees who may take paid training leave, for every hour a self-employed driver spends away from his trade, it is an hour less spent on earning a living.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, most drivers who wish to undertake training must bear triple costs – training fee, vehicle rental and loss of income.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given that many drivers have depleted their savings trying to cope with COVID-19, this is a challenging dilemma.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can the Ministry also provide an update for the support of our drivers to prepare for a better future?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Throughout COVID-19, our drivers have been frontliners and sometimes face the wrath of angry and unreasonable commuters.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This can range from ugly spats on the COVID-19 measures to our female drivers who meet the tricky passengers as they brave the long night drives.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to thank all Members for their questions and suggestions for my Ministry, which Senior Minister of State Amy Khor, Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng and I will endeavour to address.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We depend on our transportation links, domestic and international, for our lives and our livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Hence, MOT's aim is to build a Resilient, Sustainable and Inclusive Transport Hub.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I will focus my response to Members' cuts on four themes: first, the recovery of our Aviation Hub; second, our sustainability initiatives; third, keeping land transport accessible and affordable; and fourth, creating good job opportunities in the transport sector.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Many companies choose to be in Singapore because they can easily reach their customers and suppliers in our region and beyond.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To lose Changi's connectivity is to lose this key competitive advantage and our livelihoods that depend on it.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In the early stages of the pandemic, we were faced with a stark and difficult trade-off between protecting public health and opening our borders.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Fortunately, we are in a different situation today, thanks to a better understanding of the virus, well-established safe management measures and high levels of vaccination in our population.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Hence, we have been able to take careful and calibrated steps to reopen our borders.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In early 2021, the passenger volumes were at 3% of pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We introduced Vaccinated Travel Lanes (VTLs) from September last year, barely six months ago, although it feels like a lifetime.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Flights at Changi have reached 38% and city links are at 58%.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Many have, finally, been able to reunite with family and friends abroad.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Other aviation hubs, like Dubai, Qatar and Istanbul, are already at up to 70% of their pre-COVID-19 international passenger traffic.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In our region, Malaysia, Vietnam, Thailand and the Philippines have announced plans to reopen their borders to all vaccinated travellers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In short, the world is learning to live with COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We now have the confidence and opportunity to move decisively.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We are now in the first phase of this plan, launching VTLs with specific countries and regions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Just last week, we announced further VTLs with Vietnam, Greece, Malaysia, Indonesia, India and Europe.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The next phase will entail a more fundamental shift – from Vaccinated Travel Lanes to vaccinated, quarantine-free travel.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our aim is to allow all fully-vaccinated travellers from countries and regions under MOH's "Low Risk" and "General Travel" categories to enter Singapore without having to serve Stay-Home Notice (SHN) or quarantine.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This will, effectively, reopen our borders to the rest of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: MOT will work closely with the Multi-Ministry Task Force (MTF) and MOH on the timing of this transition, which will depend on the public health situation in Singapore and the world, among other things.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We share Ms Poh Li San’s concerns about the potential impact of the situation in Ukraine.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It has already affected fuel prices and could impede the recovery of the global economy and international aviation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We are monitoring the situation closely with our aviation partners and will mount an appropriate response should the need arise.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In the meantime, our airport community is gearing up for higher travel volumes.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: During the pandemic, the workforce in Changi Airport Group, SIA, SATS and other aviation companies fell sharply.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Based on MOM's latest published employment data, as of September 2021, the air transport sector employed about 25,000 workers, nearly one-third less than pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: SIA has started hiring new cabin crew and SATS is bringing back experienced workers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This is an important effort, but by no means an easy one.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Dennis Tan asked for an update on Terminal 5 (T5).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In 2020, we announced a two-year pause in the development of T5.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We have used the opportunity of this pause to review the T5 design in light of the pandemic experience and the heightened sustainability ambition.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But there should be no doubt that we are firm in our resolve that Changi must have the capacity and capability to seize opportunities that arise from aviation growth, especially in Asia, and we will provide an update on the review in due course.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Yesterday, in the Joint Segment on the Singapore Green Plan, I announced our land transport emissions target and explained how vehicle electrification will contribute to that effort.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Today, I will cover other sustainability initiatives in the transport sector.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Ms Poh Li San asked about the Sustainable Air Hub Blueprint which is key to Changi’s future competitiveness.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Blueprint will establish emissions reduction targets for 2030 and 2050 and the specific measures we will take at the airport, with airlines and in air traffic management.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: All of these can contribute to a more sustainable air hub.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Besides lowering emissions, it will also create new opportunities for Singaporeans in fields like data analytics and engineering.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The detailed plans will be announced in early 2023.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Ms Poh also asked how we will help aviation companies cope with increased business costs arising from carbon taxes, which would include higher electricity charges.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: MOT and Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS) are working with our aviation companies to adopt new technologies and other measures to enhance energy efficiency, reduce electricity usage and lower carbon emissions, such as through the deployment of solar panels at the airport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I should add that our aviation enterprises should also view this as an opportunity to differentiate themselves and enhance their competitiveness, given the global focus on sustainability.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In a similar vein, I would like to inform Mr Dennis Tan that we are making significant efforts to build a sustainable maritime hub.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: International shipping accounts for about 3% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Maritime centres like Singapore can play a meaningful role in achieving the emissions targets set by the International Maritime Organization.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As a follow-up to last year’s recommendations of the International Advisory Panel for Maritime Decarbonisation, the Maritime Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) has held extensive consultations with the industry.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This effort has culminated in the Maritime Singapore Decarbonisation Blueprint, which I am happy to launch today.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: First, we will reduce emissions from our port terminals and harbour craft.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For harbour craft that operate in our port, we will first use low-carbon fuels such as biofuels, LNG and diesel-electric hybrids.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This will enable us to reduce emissions by 15% from 2021 levels by 2030.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In parallel, we will develop and deploy zero-carbon vessels such as those using electricity, to further halve 2030's emission levels by 2050.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Second, we will support global efforts to decarbonise international shipping.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We are working with the industry, research community and international partners on R&D, pilots and standards development for low and zero carbon fuels, especially at the new Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We expect hydrogen and its carriers, including ammonia and methanol, as well as bio-LNG, to be important components of the future fuel mix.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We will, therefore, prepare our port for this multi-fuel transition.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As I shared yesterday, the adoption of EVs can make an important contribution, but the greenest modes of mobility are walking, cycling and the use of public transport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We will continue to enhance these options for commuters.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It is a critical investment in the capacity of our public transport system, the productivity of our economy and effective mobility for our people.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We are making good progress in this regard.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: LTA’s 2021 Household Travel Survey shows that seven in 10 households now live within a 10-minute walk of the nearest train station.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This brings us closer to our target of eight in 10 households by 2030.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We aim to raise this to 90% by 2040.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In August last year, we opened the second stage of the Thomson East Coast Line, or TEL.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We expect 11 more TEL stations to commence service in the second half of 2022.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This will connect residents in the north directly to many destinations in the city and significantly shorten travel times.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Those who live or work near stations like Great World, Maxwell and Shenton Way will have direct connections to the entire MRT network.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: When TEL is fully opened over the next few years, more than 240,000 households will be within a 10-minute walk from a TEL station.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Beyond the Thomson East Coast Line, the Jurong Region Line (JRL) and Cross Island Line (CRL) will open in stages from 2027 and 2030 respectively.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The JRL serves the north-western part of Singapore, connecting towns like Choa Chu Kang, Tengah and Jurong to Nanyang Technological University and the Jurong Innovation District.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For CRL, we had earlier shared details about the first stage comprising 12 stations from Aviation Park to Bright Hill, as well as the extension with three stations from Elias to Punggol.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The second stage of the Cross Island Line will extend further west and run through areas such as Turf City, Sunset Way, Clementi, West Coast and Jurong Lake District.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We will release more details later this year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Cross Island Line will have interchanges with all the radial lines, giving commuters more travel route options.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: A wider and denser network also strengthens resilience at the system level.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The rail network is complemented by bus services.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As we expand our public transport system and the asset and operating base grows, costs will inevitably rise.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: One way to sustain this growing network and manage costs is to optimise the provision of bus and rail services holistically at the system level.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Senior Minister of State Chee will elaborate on how we seek to achieve this, with a focus on the overall benefit to commuters.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng suggested giving discounts to encourage more off-peak travel.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Indeed, this is another way to better utilise our existing public transport infrastructure.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: With changing work and travel patterns, we will continue to work with employers and study various options to smoothen peak demand.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Some Members like Mr Lim Biow Chuan have pointed out that a high-quality public transport system must be resilient, yet affordable and accessible.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The challenge is in striking the difficult but essential balance, between quality, affordability and financial sustainability of our public transport system over the long term.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In particular, even as we manage increasing costs, we have always sought to keep public transport affordable for all Singaporeans, especially for vulnerable commuters like our seniors and persons with disabilities (PWDs).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Indeed, that is why we tilt public transport subsidies towards more vulnerable commuter segments.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Seniors and persons with disabilities from lower-income households can benefit from this additional support.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, when Assoc Prof Jamus Lim suggests making public transport free for seniors and persons with disabilities, we understand where he is coming from, yet do not necessarily agree with where he suggests we go.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To address the Member’s proposal, it is worthwhile to first understand what we are already doing today and what his suggestions mean for commuters and taxpayers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: On average, we subsidise more than $1 for every journey taken on public transport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As of January this year, there are around 975,000 seniors and persons with disabilities who hold concession cards, which is nearly 1 million.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Depending on the trip, they receive a discount of up to 55% from what an adult commuter would pay.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Member has estimated that his proposal will cost $300 to $400 million annually, which he has acknowledged has to be paid for by commuters or taxpayers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Using his numbers, for taxpayers, this would mean a 15% to 20% increase to the $2 billion in subsidies already borne by them.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In contrast, the Public Transport Council, or PTC, which is cognisant of the need to ensure that fares remain affordable for vulnerable commuter groups, adopts a different approach.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: When fares are increased, PTC has apportioned less of the increase to concessionary commuter groups and more to other adult commuters.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But everyone pays a share and those who can pay more, do so.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This is a more equitable approach, which has served us well over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Looking ahead, several converging trends will affect our public transport system over the next decade – a growing rail network, shifting work and travel patterns, our ageing population and volatile energy prices.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Amidst these changes, it is important to have a fare formula for long-term financial sustainability.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The current fare formula is valid until 2022.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We will commence the fare formula review this year and conclude the exercise by next year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The PTC will continue to strike a delicate balance across cost pressures faced by public transport operators, the burden on taxpayers of public transport subsidies and fare affordability for commuters.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Chairman, let me now turn to active mobility and private transport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Walking and cycling complement our public transport network, especially to bridge the first- and last-mile connections.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Many different groups of commuters use our various paths and I note the comments by several Members about the nature of the interactions in these different pathways.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These paths should not be territory that is jostled or contested over.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Rather, they should be common spaces that we share and enjoy with a culture of graciousness.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To balance the needs of different users and promote safety and graciousness, the Active Mobility Advisory Panel, or AMAP, was first formed in 2015.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng has taken over from Minister of State Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim as Chairman since the start of the new term of AMAP in January this year and he will elaborate more on the steps that we have taken and on AMAP’s key priorities going forward.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Given our limited land, we have long pursued a car-lite strategy.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The COE system is an allocation mechanism that responds to market forces.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Abdul Samad raised questions about motorcycle COEs where prices have been high in recent times.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Murali Pillai have also suggested increasing motorcycle COE supply.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I understand the reasons for their suggestions and share their concerns for those who may depend on motorcycles for a living.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: TCOEs mean that the bidder has six months.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, it is a temporary COE – six months within which they can then utilise that COE.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And the fact that, over that six-month period, the utilisation rate has been high consistently at 99% underscores the point that demand has been high.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: There have been some suggestions, like from Mr Murali Pillai, that perhaps we could consider a special sub-allocation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Several Members asked about job prospects and how we will develop local talent.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Chairman, the changes I have outlined will need the support of our transport workers and unions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The past two years have been difficult for the entire transport community, especially for our frontline workers in our airport, seaport and land transport system.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: With hard work and grit, they have kept Singapore connected.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And I want to thank the entire transport community, especially our frontline transport workers, for their tenacity and forbearance in this most challenging of times.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Beyond COVID-19, as we forge ahead with electrification, digitalisation and automation, I know that many of our workers in the workforce may be worried about their jobs and their future.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our commitment to you is that we will be with you every step of the way.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
