text: We are working with the unions and employers, our tripartite partners, to ensure that you navigate this transition successfully.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We will help you to upskill and retrain so that you can seize these new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Senior Minister of State Amy Khor and Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat will elaborate on how we will do this.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Chairman, a resilient, sustainable and inclusive transport network is essential for Singapore's survival and success and to safeguard the lives and livelihoods of our people.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our world-class Aviation Hub, Maritime Centre and land transport network of today are the fruits of the labour of earlier generations who adapted to the challenges and needs of their time while planning and investing for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The critical decisions our transport pioneers made were not necessarily conventional wisdom of the time nor were they self-evident.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Building Changi Airport, betting on containerised shipping, constructing an MRT network and introducing vehicle population control measures are just some examples.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But with the passage of time and the benefit of hindsight, we can appreciate how their decisions, some even unpopular, positioned Singapore strategically for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In the same way, the responsibility now falls upon us to steward our world-class transport ecosystem adapted to the evolving circumstances and emerging trends and, ultimately, pass on an even more resilient, sustainable and inclusive transport hub to and for future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Yong proposed that bus operators tap on taxi drivers as reserve bus captains who can be deployed during a crisis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Joan Pereira made a similar suggestion at a recent Sitting to bring back former and recently retired bus captains.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These are possible ways to increase the resilience of our public transport workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Service 22 and service 66 ran from Ang Mo Kio to Tampines and from Jurong East to Bedok respectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Service 506 was an express service from Jurong East to Upper East Coast.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As Service 22 was shortened, consequential changes were made to service 65 to serve Tampines Avenue 4.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When there are changes to bus services, commuters need time to adjust to the new arrangements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: My PAP colleagues, who look after areas affected by these changes, have also shared feedback from their residents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Earlier, Minister Iswaran spoke about the importance of financial prudence and sustainability, for our public transport system to remain resilient, affordable and accessible over the longer term.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To achieve this, we need to regularly trim and reallocate excess capacity, including bus services, when we expand our MRT network to keep overall costs manageable for commuters and taxpayers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, how does LTA decide on changes to bus services?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We start with ridership data, which is an objective indication of commuter demand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To be clear, we do operate bus services with low ridership.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are many such services which run at a loss and require funding from the $1 billion pool of bus subsidies every year because they provide necessary connectivity for commuters in some areas who otherwise would not have alternative public transport options.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We also keep some trunk services for network resilience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: However, there are bus services with low ridership that run parallel to MRT lines and have alternative bus services plying similar routes, including the three services 22, 66 and 506 that we are discussing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Their ridership numbers along some parts of the trunk route had been low and fell further after Downtown Line 3 became operational in 2017.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is because many commuters preferred to take MRT for longer journeys, using buses as feeder services for travelling to and from key transport nodes within the town.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: By switching to a combination of bus and MRT for long journeys, commuters enjoy lower fares and shorten their total travelling times, compared to taking the bus from start to end.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, a trip from Bedok North to MacPherson, after including waiting and transfers, would take around 25 minutes via feeder bus and DTL versus 42 minutes via bus service 66.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The bus-MRT option also costs less because the distance travelled is shorter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: LTA amended the route of bus service 65 in Tampines, so that commuters would still have connectivity between Tampines Avenue 4 and Bedok Reservoir Road when service 22 was shortened.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The original route for service 65 through Tampines Avenues 1 and 5 has three other bus services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: LTA will continue to explore cost reduction methods before making changes to a bus service.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This includes switching from double deck to single deck buses and reducing service frequency where possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These steps were taken for the three bus services before the decision was made in 2021 to shorten their routes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: However, the cost reductions from the above changes are not very significant as running a bus service still requires bus captains to work in shifts and a technical crew to maintain the buses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: By trimming some of the existing bus services with low ridership, we free up resources that can be reallocated to provide new feeder services for new residential estates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through these efforts, we are better able to meet new demand for bus services without a rapid increase in operating costs and subsidies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Put another way, if we continue to run the three bus services without any changes, it means that either commuters or taxpayers would have to pay an additional $9.5 million per year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Hence, I hope Mr Giam understands why we are unable to agree with him to retain as many trunk services as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will retain some as I explained, but we cannot go to the extent he has proposed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: That will not be financially prudent and sustainable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And we will not be doing what is in the best collective interests of commuters and taxpayers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We strengthened our reputation as a trusted hub port and international maritime centre (IMC).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Singapore ranked top in the 2022 Leading Maritime Cities of the World report, including for "Attractiveness and Competitiveness" and "Maritime Technology".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This achievement would not have been possible without your dedication, your contributions and your sacrifices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how we are enhancing Singapore as a reliable and resilient transport node.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Maritime Singapore will develop strong capabilities, superior connectivity and rewarding careers to address emerging challenges and seize new opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: PSA has commenced operations of its first two berths at Tuas Port as scheduled.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are making steady progress with the rest of the construction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Tuas Port will secure Singapore’s cargo connectivity to the world and keep up our competitiveness as a global hub port.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our port will leverage on technology to operate more efficiently, sustainably and safely.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MPA will use artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning to manage the increasing scale and complexity of ship movements in our waters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our next-generation Vessel Traffic Management System (VTMS) will be equipped with advanced smart collision detection capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It will be based at the future Port Operations Control Centre in Tuas, to be completed in 2025.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Another key technology is 5G telecommunications, which will support new concepts of operation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It will enable shore-to-ship deliveries using drones, which is cheaper, better and faster than the traditional method of sending a boat and crew; or piloting a containership safely from a control room on shore. 5G will support our vision to be the Silicon Valley of Marine Tech and be a game-changer to differentiate our port and IMC from the competition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will also help maritime SMEs build capabilities to ride the digitalisation wave.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We currently provide funding support under the Sea Transport Industry Digital Plan (IDP) and this is given to SMEs in the ship agency, harbour craft and bunkering sub-sectors to help them implement digital solutions to improve their operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will expand IDP to cover all SMEs in the Sea Transport sector, including those providing ship supply services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MPA will also extend the grant beyond end 2022, to benefit eligible maritime companies on an ongoing basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Next, we will expand our physical and digital connectivity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Tuas Port will be the nucleus of a larger ecosystem of business and industrial districts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We can enhance the connectivity of high-value sectors like advanced manufacturing and cold chain logistics by locating such companies close to the port.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government has set aside land around Tuas Port for companies to integrate their developments with the port.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will also review our regulatory processes to maximise the benefits from integration and process efficiency.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOT will leverage on our strengths as an air and sea hub to expand the suite of connectivity options for cargo owners, including multimodal options.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Such air-sea cargo solutions provide additional efficiency and resilience and support just-in-time manufacturing and distribution for regional supply chains.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In the information age, digital connectivity is as important as physical connectivity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Electronic bills of lading (eBLs) are documents proving ownership of cargo in transit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The benefits of eBLs over physical documents are clear: receive cargo faster, free up working capital and have more secure transactions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: However, adoption of eBLs has been slow due to legal and technical hurdles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MPA will co-fund three consortiums to develop and trial eBL solutions across the container, wet bulk and dry bulk segments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through these trials, we aim to grow the ecosystem and encourage adoption of eBLs in Singapore and beyond.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: With the expansion in capabilities and connectivity, Maritime Singapore will grow and create rewarding career opportunities for our people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Looking at our progress so far, there is scope to grow even more good jobs by 2025, if conditions remain favourable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As Mr Yong noted, it is important to attract more local workers to take up both seafaring and shore-based jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MPA is supporting the industry and unions to attract talent, nurture our workforce and transform workplaces in Maritime Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Seafaring experience is important in the maritime sector and can open doors to good shore-based careers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Captain Ranesh Sandhu started out as a seafarer in Neptune Orient Lines and became a ship master after a decade of sailing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: His seafaring credentials have laid the foundations for a meaningful shore-based career, including in leadership positions such as Senior Director of Shipping for Marathon Petroleum Corporation and Managing Director at BTS Tankers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MPA has partnered the Singapore Maritime Officers’ Union (SMOU), the Singapore Organisation of Seamen (SOS) and maritime companies to attract and develop locals for seafaring careers through scholarships and awards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Local seafarers like my Toa Payoh resident, Mr Takamasa Ng, have benefited from the Tripartite Maritime Scholarship (TMSS).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Takamasa obtained his Class 3 Certificate of Competency (CoC) in 2018.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: He currently works on board a ship for NYK Line and he wants to continue sailing and attain his Class 1 CoC, which is the highest level of certification.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Qualifying as an experienced seafarer is a long and challenging journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Attaining the Class 1 CoC can take eight years or more and the job requires frequent stints away from home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will support our local seafarers on this journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This helps to support their income when they are not sailing, so they can continue to upgrade their seafaring skills and knowledge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I hope this will encourage more local mechanical engineers to become marine engineers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have also collaborated with Yellow Ribbon Singapore to place suitable inmates as trainees with harbour craft operators to become steersmen or engine drivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Eight ex-offenders have benefited so far and we hope to increase the number over time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is especially important for an international industry like maritime, which requires openness and connectivity to thrive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Singapore cannot be a hub for maritime, aviation, finance or technology, if we adopt populist manpower policies, build walls around us and disconnect ourselves from the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We cannot aim to be a hub and yet become inward-looking.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There is no such thing as an inward-looking hub.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Foreign talents bring new capabilities and perspectives that keep our hub dynamic and they complement our Singaporean Core.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The tripartite partners fully support this approach, as we understand that a good local-foreign complement is necessary to grow our economy and create good jobs for our people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Chairman, I will speak about MOT’s efforts to improve Singapore’s land transport system, in four aspects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: First, I will touch on how we have transformed the taxi and private hire car sector and made it more resilient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Second, I will share on how we leverage technology to improve the resilience and reliability of our road network, and how we prepare for new shifts from these technologies, like vehicle electrification.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Third, I will explain how we are reshaping our transport infrastructure by focusing on people and sustainability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Our land transport sector has remained resilient through the pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This stems largely from the courage and dedication of our frontline workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Taxi and private hire car drivers took extra precautions such as regularly disinfecting their vehicles even as ridership plunged.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To tide them through, the Government, associations and operators provided targeted financial support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We expect this to rise further but will continue to monitor the situation closely.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: If necessary, we will step in again to support our drivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling will be glad to know that we go beyond financial support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will improve our service delivery to drivers, with the launch of the digital vocational licences in the second quarter of this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Prospective drivers will receive their digital licences in about half the time, from around 20 days today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Drivers no longer need to worry about losing their vocational licences, as they can easily access it through Singpass.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We also agree that drivers should feel safe.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Indeed, taxi and private hire car drivers are covered as public service workers under the Protection from Harassment Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We stand ready to support drivers who encounter abusive passengers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Chairman, our land transport system is in the midst of a major transition – towards vehicle electrification.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: A wide range of industries will be affected and workers, such as workshop technicians, must upskill to remain competitive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Government is, therefore, actively consulting OEMs, fleet owners and other industry partners to better understand the training needs of these workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The aim is to equip them with the necessary skills to seize these new opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Our taxi fleet will also be increasingly electrified.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To prepare drivers, LTA will launch an updated training curriculum for taxi and private hire vocational licences this month.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The refreshed curriculum will cover electric vehicles and the latest on-the-road competencies, such as the use of mapping and navigational tools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Our public transport workers will also receive support to be future-ready.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Melvin Yong would know, we want to ensure that public transport workers, young or old, are ready to seize new opportunities arising from the greening of our fleet.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Singapore Bus Academy has conducted 17 runs of cleaner energy bus training programmes since December 2019, involving over 550 workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: While preparing for the future, there are core functions that LTA must continue to perform, such as the maintenance of the expanding rail, road and footpath infrastructure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As Mr Gan Thiam Poh shared, technology can help us be more efficient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: One example is the use of video analytics and artificial intelligence in the maintenance of our 9,500-odd lane kilometres of roads.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: LTA has trialled the use of highspeed cameras mounted onto a van to automatically detect and report defects on the road since 2020.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Defects are automatically logged backend, to enable targeted, predictive maintenance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: When fully implemented, the technology-enhanced process can reduce manhours by up to 30%.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Beyond leveraging technology, we will build more sustainable transport infrastructure, in collaboration with our communities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The greenest way to travel is by walking, cycling and using public transport.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: That is why we have several Transit Priority Corridors, or TPCs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This may not sound like a lot, but each TPC will become the key thoroughfare for the neighbourhood.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: An example of an upcoming TPC is along Sin Ming Avenue, between Upper Thomson Road and Marymount Road.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Wider footpaths, new cycling paths and bus lanes will be incorporated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Residents in the area can more seamlessly ride a bus, walk or cycle to the amenities near them, such as schools and the Bright Hill MRT station.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao will be glad to know that we have made good progress in reimagining our road spaces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We widened the footpaths along a busy stretch of Havelock Road, where there are several popular eateries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Residents and visitors now find it a safer and more comfortable walking experience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have also transformed the Civic District as we closed Connaught Drive, Fullerton Road and Anderson Bridge to vehicular traffic.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This will create a safer environment for pedestrians, especially for seniors and children.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will also begin pedestrianisation trials for Eng Hoon Street to create space for community use.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These ideas were shaped in consultation with the local community including residents, shop owners and the Tiong Bahru Market and Hawkers’ Association.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: LTA will work with URA to co-create placemaking ideas with the local community that will be implemented through the Lively Places Programme.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: URA had earlier announced the pilot Business Improvement District programme to drive placemaking efforts.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To complement this, LTA will lead an inter-agency workgroup to study plans to enhance the pedestrian and cycling experience.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Key areas of focus include connectivity to transport nodes, conversion of road spaces for wider footpaths and cycling paths and community activities.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These repurposing projects are connected by a common thread – the active input from local communities.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Going forward and in the spirit of inclusivity and citizen participation, this approach will be our modus operandi.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Illegally modified vehicles are dangerous to motorists and pedestrians and many of them cause noise disturbances as Mr Gan pointed out.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To ensure roadworthiness of vehicles and compliance to in-use noise emission standards, LTA mandates periodic vehicle inspections.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: LTA also conducts joint enforcement operations with other agencies to flush out these vehicles.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: During a joint enforcement conducted in December 2021, LTA officers issued summons for 34 vehicles for offences including illegal modifications.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Two workshops were charged last year for providing illegal modification services.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our approach to safety must take cognisance of society's changing needs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Given our ageing population, LTA has implemented Silver Zones at towns with a higher senior population since 2014.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Key measures implemented include reduced speed limits and narrower roads to slow traffic.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They have proven effective, reducing the accident rate of senior pedestrians by about 80%.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To date, LTA has completed 22 Silver Zones.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Agencies have also been working to improve the safety of workers transported on lorries.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Yong asked for an update on this.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We understand the union's and NGOs' concerns and likewise want to improve safety for workers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To protect lives and livelihoods, we need to take a balanced approach and make changes that are sustainable.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is why we consulted extensively on this issue, including with trade associations in the construction sector, such as Singapore Contractors Association Limited, the marine and process sectors and private bus operators.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Many small and medium enterprises, especially in the specialist trade, shared with us the constraints they face.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They may need to transport a small crew with bulky equipment to several different locations in a single day.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It will be operationally challenging and inefficient for them to use buses for workers and separately transport their equipment in lorries.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In addition, in our engagements with private bus operators, they have told us that there are simply insufficient private buses and drivers to transport the large number of workers in the manufacturing and construction, marine and process sectors, especially when other activities like tourism resume post-COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: A full transition to buses could require a doubling or even tripling of the number of large private buses in the industry today!

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Even if multiple and staggered trips are made, the demand for buses will still be significant.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Furthermore, bus operators shared that the shortage of bus drivers would be an even more binding constraint.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These challenges are not all insurmountable, but we will need time to work through them with the industry and relevant agencies.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The good news is that some firms have already shifted away from using lorries for some projects.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, Tong Tar Transport was asked by a multinational construction company to ferry about 3,000 workers of their main and sub-contractors between dormitories to the construction site via buses.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This was a large-scale endeavour that involved coordination among various bus operators but shows that it is possible under the right circumstances.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We encourage more in the industry to follow.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will facilitate the sharing of best practices and will study the "conditions for success" to enable more companies to make the shift.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In the meantime, we have identified two areas to further improve the safety of workers on lorries.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: First, the Government will require all lorries to be subjected to some form of speed management device.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Today, speed limiters are already mandated for all goods vehicles with maximum laden weight (MLW) of 12 tonnes and above.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: TP will be engaging the industry closely on this and will release more details when ready.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Second, besides ensuring the relevant hardware is in place, it is crucial to ensure that lorry drivers operate safely behind the wheel at all times.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Some have also suggested requiring lorries to be fitted with seat belts.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We recently consulted the motor vehicle dealers and workshops again.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Their feedback remains that retrofitting seat belts would not be feasible and could in fact pose safety risks.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Commercial lorries today are not designed for seat belts to be installed in the rear deck, as the floorboards in the rear deck might not be sufficiently strong to keep the seat belts anchored in the event of an accident.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: There are also liability issues for such modifications without the support of the lorry manufacturers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Without the industry being able to bring in lorries with seat belts and vouch for their safety, it is not prudent to mandate this.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Lastly, we have heard calls to mandate rain covers to lorry rear decks to shield workers from the elements.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But we will take this one step further.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will continue to study further measures even as industries adapt and more companies move towards alternative modes of transport.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Once again, I urge employers to do their part in ensuring the welfare and safety of their staff.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Together we can look forward to a more sustainable, vibrant and safe land transport system!

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Mr Chairman, Minister Iswaran spoke about our plans to transform Singapore into a resilient, sustainable and inclusive transport hub.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: To support a shift towards greener choices, I am going to cover the two transport modes that have the lowest carbon emission: active mobility and public transport.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In particular, I will share how we will continue to invest in both the "hardware" and "heartware".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: First, Mr Ang Wei Neng, Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Ms Poh Li San will be pleased to hear about our efforts to enhance our cycling path network.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Despite the pandemic, we have accelerated the plans for the Islandwide Cycling Network.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These are not easy infrastructure projects, especially in mature towns where there is little space on the sidewalk and various utilities underground.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This will greatly improve convenience and connectivity both within and between towns.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: A good example of connectivity within a town is Bukit Panjang, where LTA is on track to complete seven kilometres of cycling paths this year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: By then, residents can cycle to Bukit Panjang Hawker Centre for lunch, continue to Zhenghua Community Club for activities and then to Bukit Panjang Integrated Transport Hub to take a bus or train.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Active mobility users and pedestrians will also enjoy the perks of improved connectivity between towns.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Once the North-South Corridor is completed, it will connect to the park connector network and local cycling paths within HDB towns along the entire corridor.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Someone living in Woodlands can cycle along dedicated paths all the way to work or play in the Rochor area.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will also increase the number of end-of-trip facilities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Today, we have about 27,000 bicycle parking lots at public transport nodes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will provide 3,000 more at MRT stations by 2025.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We are encouraging workplaces to provide such facilities through the Active Commute Grant and have awarded the grant to 14 workplaces so far.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We hope that more workplaces will make good use of this grant when the next round of applications open this year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Next, like Mr Dennis Tan suggested, education and enforcement of our rules must go hand in hand.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: To reduce the risk of severe accidents, we have put in place regulations that are reviewed regularly with the support of the Active Mobility Advisory Panel (AMAP) in consultation with the public.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Over the years, we have imposed speed limits on paths and set restrictions on the weight and size of devices.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: At the start of this year, to enhance safety of on-road cycling, we introduced a guideline on safe passing distance between motorists and cyclists, and a new rule to limit cycling group size on roads.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: However, we heard the desire of cyclists to cycle in larger groups.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: More details will be shared at a later date.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We have stepped up enforcement efforts to deter errant riders since the ban of e-scooters on footpaths in 2019.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We have also leveraged technology to identify hotspots for enforcement, many thanks to public feedback from the MyTransport app.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: To ensure riders of personal mobility devices (PMDs) and power-assisted bicycles are familiar with active mobility rules, we have introduced mandatory theory tests.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: A significant number considering that we have a population of about 40,000 registered devices.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: At the same time, like Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Dr Shahira Abdullah pointed out, public education is key.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: LTA and the Traffic Police are working together to raise awareness among cyclists and motorists through campaigns, and we are also looking to incorporate these materials into the driving theory test curriculum.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Third, an inclusive active mobility system requires a gracious and responsible community, underpinned by clear and forward-looking regulations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Since 2016, the AMAP led by Minister of State Muhammad Faishal has played an important role in building a safe and gracious active mobility landscape.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The AMAP strikes a balance among the many competing needs of different users in consultation with the public.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: As the new AMAP chairman, I would like to share two key priorities for this new term.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: First, we will stay ahead of emerging trends that could shape the active mobility landscape.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For instance, we will review the use of devices, such as cargo bikes and trikes which have gained popularity overseas and are starting to enter the local market.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will also review the safe use of recumbent bikes and personal mobility aids.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Second, we will continue to strengthen our engagement and education efforts to collectively build a safe and gracious culture on our paths and roads.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Many stakeholders have responded positively in partnering us.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For instance, public bus operators have emphasised to their bus captains the importance of defensive driving and keeping a lookout for road cyclists.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Earlier this year, a few cyclists from the Singapore Cycling Federation tried out bus simulators to better appreciate the perspective and challenges of bus captains.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Last year, LTA also launched the new Confidence on Wheels Programme to equip active mobility riders with practical riding skills and to promote safe riding habits.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will build on the momentum set forth by the AMAP to expand and deepen our partnerships with the community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Next, I will share about our progress towards an inclusive public transport system.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This tool contains pictures and keywords that commuters can point to so that public transport staff understand their needs more easily.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Besides the deaf or hard-of-hearing community, this should also be useful to commuters who have other communication difficulties.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Second, we have installed the Hearing Enhancement System at Passenger Service Centres, starting with those at the Thomson-East Coast Line.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The system reduces background noise so that commuters with hearing aids can communicate better with station staff.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: More than five million trips are made on public transport every day.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We hope that the millions of eyes and ears can help to look out for people who show signs of dementia and are lost.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Members of public can bring them to these Go-To-Points and enlist the help of our staff who are trained in dementia awareness.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Everyone can do a part to help commuters with dementia who lose their way to be reunited with their loved ones quickly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The third group is families with young children.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We currently have baby care rooms at all interchange stations on the Thomson-East Coast Line and 60% of our bus interchanges.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: To achieve a truly inclusive public transport system, we must also cultivate our "heartware".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Tasked with this mission, the Caring SG Commuters Committee has collaborated with partners on various initiatives, such as by engaging different profiles of commuters on the ground, including those with invisible disabilities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I will urge all of us to adopt four caring behaviours in our daily journeys: give time, give care, give a hand and give thanks.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: How else can we play a part in this journey?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We can become Caring Commuter Champions to better assist commuters in need.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For her university's final year project, Ashley had researched about wayfinding for persons with visual impairment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: She has benefited from the Champions training on how to assist other profiles of commuters.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: As a Champion, she hopes to encourage more people to lend a helping hand to others.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: While the Committee has laid a good foundation, all of us must play our part.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Moving forward, the Committee will deepen stakeholders' involvement at the individual, enterprise and community levels to facilitate more ground-up initiatives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to say a few words in Mandarin.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: (In Mandarin):   We have spared no efforts to build an inclusive public transport system that is a choice mode for all.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Over the years, we have enhanced our infrastructure so that all commuters, including persons with disabilities, the elderly and families travelling with young children, can navigate the public transport system more easily.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: However, a truly inclusive public transport system is not built on infrastructure enhancements alone, but also requires a gracious and caring commuting culture.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: By giving time, giving care, giving a hand and giving thanks to others during our daily commute, we can all make a positive difference to our fellow commuters' journeys.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: (In English): Mr Chairman, people are at the heart of what we do, in connecting people, places and possibilities through our different transport modes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will continue to invest in both our hardware and heartware.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I urge everyone to play our part towards a gracious culture to spin wheels of virtuous cycles that will make every journey on our paths and public transport a safe and inclusive one for all.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Currently, the agencies are looking into imposing demerit points in addition to fines for offenders who knowingly drive an illegally modified vehicle.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And we continue to undertake investigations on workshops who provide such services.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And for feeder services, after bus 66 was re-routed, my residents were left with only bus 228 as a feeder service to Bedok Interchange.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many have told me that the intervals of 15 minutes or more are really too long and LTA would be aware of this because I have written many letters on behalf of my residents on this matter.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, can LTA increase the frequency of feeder bus services to make up for the reduction in other services?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, while I agree there is a need for financial prudence, we must not be penny wise and pound foolish.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If more commuters take public transport instead of private transport, it will lower our carbon footprint and reduce traffic congestion.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, does MOT take this into account when it reduces the bus services?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Member for his questions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I have a clarification for him, because he has heard the explanations that I and also Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat have given in terms of the process and how we go about this.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, may I understand, does he accept the principle that as we expand our rail network and as we invest more, and as the capital base and the asset base grow, we have an obligation to optimise across the system?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Is he disagreeing with us on the principle or is it about the process?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Or is it specifically about the outcome in his constituency?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I do not disagree with the principle that we must optimise, but I disagree with how it is sometimes optimised.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Because I feel that sometimes, for example, for trunk services, yes, there is a need to ensure that the services are not running empty.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: But there is a small group of people – the elderly, disabled – who need to travel for long distances and they find it very inconvenient to transfer a lot.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, that is why I am asking, as a compromise, can mini or smaller buses be used?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Member for that clarification.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is helpful because it means that we agree in principle that we have a fiscal responsibility to see what we can do to optimise the resources.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat would be able to give more information on his specific points about trunk routes and alternatives.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But the Member also raised the point about financial prudence and about being penny wise and pound foolish.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think it is all about big pounds that are at stake.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: When I listen to some of the comments from Mr Giam and also his colleague Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, I am reminded that, Mr Chairman, with your indulgence, there is an Ernest Hemingway book “The Sun Also Rises”.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In it, there is a character Mike Campbell and he is asked, “How did you go bankrupt?” And he replies, “Two ways – gradually, then suddenly.” I think we need to remember this: if we resist every effort to optimise and if we champion every effort to increase services or collect less, but resist every effort to perhaps increase fares and other measures to have the financial resources to do what we need to do, then, what we will end up with is this – the creep will be gradual and the end will be sudden.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, what we are trying to do here – and I think I am not the first Transport Minister to make this point; it has been made by generations of Transport Ministers and I am sure many more to come – is really to strike that all-essential balance.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I do not think there is a monopoly of virtue here, in terms of wanting to help Singaporeans, especially those who are in vulnerable segments, but what we are trying to do is make sure that we are being fair to our commuters, to our taxpayers, to the vulnerable segments and also, to public transport operators and their financial viability.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Chairman, I will address some of the more specific points that Mr Giam mentioned.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Specifically, on service 228, I touched on feeder services in my speech earlier.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For service 228, Mr Giam did give us some feedback because initially, when the bus services were shortened, what LTA then tried to do was precisely like what he mentioned – make sure that we have bus service 228 to provide the connectivity to the necessary key transport nodes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: When Mr Giam shared the feedback with us, we then followed up with the bus operators to make improvements and adjustments to bus service 228.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Just to share some data, in terms of the loading level and the waiting time.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This was not excessive, but it would feel more crowded than usual.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In fact, on most days, and I am referring to peak periods, it is around 25%.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, the situation has improved and I want to thank Mr Giam for sharing his feedback with us to enable us to be able to address some of these local concerns.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: About waiting times, Sir, service 228, I do not think what Mr Giam said earlier is factually correct.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, the frequency is actually every five minutes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There is another way to help residents to shorten the waiting time, so they do not have to go to the bus stop too early.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is to help them to use the MyTransport app.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I understand, maybe some of the seniors may not be so familiar with technology, but that is also an area where, collectively, as a community, we can reach out to them through raising awareness and public education, help them to be able to use these tools, so that they can plan their journeys, they can shorten the waiting time.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And, I think, importantly, the shift that I was explaining in my main speech will allow us to provide new feeder services to new areas, meeting the needs of other commuters.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, yes, we want to take care of as many commuters as possible, but our responsibility is not just to one group of commuters, but to all commuters, collectively.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We do need to weigh difficult trade-offs and make the adjustments accordingly.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think I do need to point out that because we shift from bigger buses to smaller buses, it does not mean the cost will shrink correspondingly.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I explained in my speech we still need to have bus captains to drive the buses in shifts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We still need to have a maintenance crew to be able to maintain the bus fleet.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In fact, if we buy new mini buses, we would have to incur additional upfront costs to buy the buses and train a new group of bus captains and a new group of technical crew to maintain these mini buses.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, from a logistics and maintenance cost point of view, I am not sure that will actually end up with lower costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I feel I should clarify that the proposal that I had explicitly states that the subsidy should be borne by MOT expenditures, not by other riders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: He spent quite a bit of time, I felt, attacking a little bit of a straw man.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is fair to say that $300 million, $400 million is not a chump change, but as I also mentioned in my speech, we should be clear that this is about 3% to 4% an increase in the Ministry’s budget, when you set it within context.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I did also seek a compromise and this was not touched on in Minister Iswaran’s clarification.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The marginal costs in this case are likely to be minimal, mainly in the form of foregone revenues, since buses and trains are already operating with spare capacity in this case.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And in fact, during the description of what happened during COVID-19, ex-Transport Minister Ong Ye Kung mentioned that buses were ferrying air.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I wonder if instead of ferrying air, could we instead ferry the elderly and the disabled in our society?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because, fundamentally, there is a need to explain where the money is going to come from.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And then, he says it is 3% to 4% of the Ministry’s budget.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I would urge the Member to look at the budget carefully.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: What the Member is proposing, is a recurrent operational subsidy of $300 million to $400 million.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, in other words, it is on the lower base which we are looking at.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think it is something we should debate.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But I think then, we should also, to be intellectually rigorous, examine where the Member and his party stand when it comes to sources of revenue.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Last year, we increased fare revenue and I know that the Leader of the Opposition made a point about how fares have increased and that is contributing to cost of living.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In other words, the Workers’ Party looks askance at increases of fares.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And yet, we are also arguing about spending more.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And the Member and his party also take a dim view of several of the revenue sources that have been proposed by the Finance Minister.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And it is by no means a straw man.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Minister Iswaran mentioned that about one-third of our airport workers have already left the airport sector, given the pandemic situation and we know that in the Airport, many frontline jobs are actually filled by foreign workers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: So, my question is that given the border closures or the border restrictions, how can Government further help airport companies get ready and ensure that we have sufficient workers prepared for the recovery of the aviation sector?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: The second question is for Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: During these peak periods where the cyclists are rushing, there could be a surge in the traffic and that may lead to safety concerns, especially against pedestrians who are using the same stretch.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: So, I hope that there will be some prioritisation of the building of such last mile stretches in the cycling network.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Chairman, if I may, I omitted to respond to a specific point that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim made which was on whether we could consider off-peak measures which, I think, was one of his ideas.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But again, I just want to make the point that when you run a concession fare system, then, basically, what it means is, you pay one concession fee and then you can vary the terms, but then the revenue level is there.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But once we say we are switching from off-peak to peak and so on, then essentially, it changes the construct and we have to look at this quite carefully.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I just wanted to make the point.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I would not rule out any options going forward because, as I have said, there are various factors that we have to take into account in thinking through our fare formula and our approach.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But I just wanted to make that point specifically.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I want to thank the Member Ms Poh Li San for her question.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Indeed, she has raised a very important point because it is one thing to say we want to increase our arrivals to 50% or more of pre-COVID-19 levels, but how to make it happen?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because there has been a significant attrition in manpower and we have to re-employ.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: MOT and CAAS are working with the unions and with the companies, first, of course, to see how many Singaporeans we can bring back into the fold.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But at the same time, a significant portion of the attrition has been manpower from overseas.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we are also working with MOM to see what kind of solutions we can put in place because once we decide to go towards vaccinated quarantine-free travel, the volumes will pick up significantly and we need to make sure that, from a capacity perspective, we are geared up.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The ability to bring in the requisite level of manpower is key and we are working with the companies and MOM on that.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Oh, a reply from Mr Baey Yam Keng.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: As we plan the roll-out, we will look at the last-mile connectivity, especially to places where many residents go to.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: So, in the Bukit Panjang example I quoted, the CC, the transport hub or hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: We must also plan it such a way that there is connectivity amongst the different stretches of cycling paths so that it makes sense for cyclists to be able to enjoy a more seamless cycling path network.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Pritam Singh, if you can keep it to a minute, so that we can have a minute’s response.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I did not intend to rise, but I had to, after the Minister for Transport stood up and spoke of "intellectually rigorous".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think he was going to say "intellectually honest" but he stopped himself and said "intellectually rigorous alternative proposals".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is not as if the money is going to come from an unknown source.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, I just wanted to clarify that point, that the party put up four different levers to consider where additional revenues can come from to address some of the issues we have raised, not just here by Member Jamus Lim, but also in our manifesto.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think it is important for me to put that out.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Leader of the Opposition for the clarification.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Intellectual rigour, intellectual honesty – I am not sure, I mean the Leader of the Opposition appears to be imputing words.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Whatever it is, I think you cannot have rigour without honesty.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In terms of proposals, I do not intend to canvass again the arguments about the different sources of revenue.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think they have been well discussed in the main Budget Debate on the Budget policies and so on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: However, I want to bring it back to this Ministry’s budget because it is an important point.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat, if you can withdraw your amendment, please.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, the state of our air, sea and land transport is a reflection of our economic and the social state of our country.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, in other words, a wide range of exciting opportunities in the transport sector.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Before I withdraw my amendment, I would like to thank Members for their 30-plus cuts and many thanks to Minister Iswaran, Senior Minister of State Amy Khor, Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat and Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng for their responses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And also the Permanent Secretary of MOT and his team and our MOT family of agencies – CAAS, MPA, LTA.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And most importantly, to all our frontline workers in the transport sector.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think they have put in a huge effort, not just over the last year but over the past two years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have been saying this for the previous Budget cuts and discussions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, all their hard work, conviction and passion to keep our air, sea and land hubs working well and going forward, being future-ready.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With that, Chairman, I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
